title: routineRun and the triggers
bridge: routineRun is like one reusable GitHub Actions job that every routine calls with its own inputs. Except: it is a Temporal workflow, so it can wait for days and survive restarts. Its ID is the root cause, so a second event with the same cause joins the open run instead of starting another.
intro: Every routine runs the same workflow, routineRun. This lesson writes it, then wires the three ways it starts. A small Action reports red CI, the Jira poll finds triaged Bugs, and schedules start the crews. No new public webhook anywhere.

sections.h: routineRun, part 1: Nova's activities, two signals
p: Routines must not fork Nova. So routineRun reuses ticketToPr's activities unchanged: acquireSandbox, workInSandbox and releaseSandbox from G3. The PR half of ticketToPr (scope judge, draft PR, Byte, findings, ready) moves into a child workflow, shipPr, that both use. Agree that split with the G4 owner.

A signal is a message sent to a running workflow (lesson p7-3). addTrigger lets another event with the same root cause join the run. decidePlan carries the same Slack Approve, Change and Stop buttons as Nova, for the bug fixers' plans.
The timeouts are safety nets. The 7-day start-to-close timeout and 5-minute heartbeats only catch a dead worker; they never limit the work.
sections.because: We reuse Nova's activities and its PR half, so the walls and review layers are built once for every routine.

sections.h: routineRun, part 2: gather, gate, work, ship
p: The body reads in order. Collect triggers, load the charter, wait the gather window, ask the gate. Then claim a VM, work, release it, and either save the shadow result or ship a PR.

preRunGate checks, in order: G3's kill switch, routine:<name>:paused, incident mode (lesson g5-4) and one open PR per routine (lesson g5-3). A gate that says wait parks the run on a timer and never starts a VM.

In shadow, nothing is opened: the diff and the proof go to S3 for the weekly comparison. Otherwise the run creates or links a Jira ticket first, so the PR title reads [FE] RH-1234 and add-jira-links works.
sections.because: The gate runs before acquireSandbox, so a paused routine or a storm never costs a VM.

sections.h: Root cause as the workflow ID, part 1
p: When main goes red, every push and every PR fails the same way. One run per root cause is the first wall against a storm of agents. The trick is to compute the workflow ID from the cause.

The trigger service lives behind POST /v1/events in the orchestrator service on inf-rhinohealth, on node:http like Byte's broker. It is internal only, so there is still no new public webhook. Callers prove who they are with GitHub OIDC: issuer, audience rhino-ai-agents, an allow-listed repository, and the trigger workflow on main as job_workflow_ref.
It never trusts the request body. It re-reads the run by run_id through the broker, read-only. That gives the failing jobs and each job's first error line.
sections.because: An ID made from the root cause turns many red events into one run without any locking code.

sections.h: Root cause as the workflow ID, part 2
p: Signal-with-start sends a signal to the workflow with that ID, and starts it first if it is not running (lesson p7-4). So the first red push starts the run, and the next ones join it.

The fingerprint uses the last green commit, the failing job names and each normalized first error. The last green commit does not move while main stays red, so later pushes give the same ID. Normalizing drops what changes between runs of the same failure: hashes and numbers.
REJECT_DUPLICATE means a closed run's ID cannot start again. A root cause that returns after its run closed is likely ping-pong. It goes to a person in #ai-agents-alerts, never to a new run.
sections.because: We send a second event for the same cause into the open run, and send a returning cause to a person.

sections.h: The trigger Action, part 1: when it runs
p: A small workflow in fcp wakes the CI and upgrade fixers. workflow_run fires when another workflow finishes; we watch the four CI workflows and keep failures on main or renovate/ branches.

It runs on fcp-runner-set, which lives inside inf-rhinohealth, so it reaches the internal trigger service. It holds no secret. id-token: write lets it ask GitHub for an OIDC token, a short-lived signed statement of which repo and workflow it is.
Cloud, client and SDK CI run on push to every branch, so Renovate branches get checks without a PR. Frontend CI runs on pull_request.
sections.because: A tiny Action on our own runners, with no secrets and no PR code, is the safest bridge to the orchestrator.

code.text:
# .github/workflows/ai-agents-routine-trigger.yml (fcp): sketch
name: "[AI-AGENTS] - Routine trigger"
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["[FRONTEND] - CI", "[CLOUD] - CI", "[CLIENT] - CI", "[SDK] - CI"]
    types: [completed]

permissions:
  id-token: write   # the OIDC token proves "this workflow, in RhinoHealth/fcp" to the trigger service
  contents: read

jobs:
  report:
    if: >-
      github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'failure' &&
      (github.event.workflow_run.head_branch == 'main' ||
       startsWith(github.event.workflow_run.head_branch, 'renovate/'))
    runs-on: fcp-runner-set   # inside inf-rhinohealth, so it reaches the internal trigger service
    steps:

sections.h: The trigger Action, part 2: report, nothing else
p: The step never checks out code and never puts event fields into a shell. Fields like a branch name come from the event and could be crafted by an attacker. Read in JavaScript from context.payload, they stay data, so nothing can be injected.
A workflow_run workflow only fires from the default branch's copy. Test it after merge with a planted failure on a throwaway branch named renovate/test-trigger, while every routine is in shadow.
Copy the file into infrastructure and gitops for the pipeline fixer, on their own runner sets. This Action only reports: the orchestrator never calls workflow_dispatch and never re-runs jobs.
sections.because: Event fields are untrusted input, so they stay in JavaScript variables and never reach a shell.

notes.text: The rule for this step: no code from the repo, no expressions pasted into the script.
Runs JavaScript with context and core ready. Pin it by SHA like the other Actions.
The repo variable AI_AGENTS_TRIGGER_URL: the internal address of the trigger service.
The finished run, read as a JavaScript object.
An OIDC token for the audience rhino-ai-agents. The service checks it.
POST /v1/events with the token as a Bearer header.
Only the run's ID and repo. The service re-reads everything else.
A non-2xx answer fails this job, so a broken bridge shows up red.

sections.h: Jira Bugs and schedules, part 1: the bug poll
p: Bug tickets are the most important trigger. They reuse G3-28's Jira poll registry, like Nova's hand-off (lesson g4-1), so there is one Jira mechanism and still no public webhook. The poll runs every 5 minutes, which is enough for bugs.

Each match starts bugfix:RH-1240 on the ai-agents-bugfix queue through startRun, so a repeat poll is a no-op. Anyone can opt a bug out with the label no-routine. If a person takes the ticket during a run, the run gets a stop signal, posts what it found, and ends.

PHI never enters a prompt. The broker's Jira scope returns summary, description and comments, never attachments. Agree with Security (Ronen) on a label for tickets that might hold customer data, and add it to the JQL.
sections.because: Reusing the poll registry keeps one tested way to read Jira and one run per ticket.

sections.h: Jira Bugs and schedules, part 2: the crews
p: Scheduled routines and housekeeping jobs run from Temporal schedules (lesson p7-5). They are the dead-code sweep, the KB ingest, the idle close, the digest, the trust ladder and the shadow report. All at odd minutes, in the Asia/Jerusalem time zone; 0-4 in cron means Sunday to Thursday.

ensureCronSchedules runs at worker start next to G3-28's ensureSchedules. It creates each schedule, or updates it if it exists. Overlap SKIP means a slow run never stacks a second one. Weekly code-health routines run on Sunday.
sections.because: Schedules in code, created idempotently at start, mean a deploy is the only way a crew's timetable changes.

quiz.q: main is red. Ten minutes later a second push fails the same job with the same first error. What happens?

options.text: A second routineRun starts for the new push
options.why: Same last green commit, same jobs, same normalized error: the same fingerprint, so the same ID.

options.text: Signal-with-start finds the open run with that ID and adds the trigger to it
options.why: One run per root cause: the second event joins through addTrigger.

options.text: The trigger service drops it because it is a duplicate
options.why: It is not dropped. It joins the open run as another trigger.

quiz.q: Why does the trigger Action read the branch name in JavaScript instead of with ${{ }} in a shell?

options.text: JavaScript is faster than bash on the runner
options.why: Speed is not the point. Safety is.

options.text: A branch name is attacker-controlled input; pasted into a shell it could run commands
options.why: Read from context.payload, it stays a string. That is how script injection is avoided.

options.text: ${{ }} expressions do not work in workflow_run workflows
options.why: They work, which is exactly why they are dangerous inside run scripts.

quiz.q: Where does the bug fixer's trigger come from?

options.text: A Jira webhook to a new public URL
options.why: There is no new public webhook. The poll reads Jira.

options.text: G3-28's Jira poll registry: triaged Bugs every 5 minutes, one run per ticket through startRun
options.why: The same mechanism as Nova's hand-off, with the team label in the JQL.
That Action reports CI failures, not Jira tickets.
